module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 50

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/50](https://www.erdosproblems.com/50)
* [Er95] Erdős, Paul, Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and geometry.
Resenhas (1995), 165-186.
* [Sch38] Schoenberg, I. J. "On asymptotic distributions of arithmetical functions."
Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 39.2 (1936): 315-330.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Set MeasureTheory Topology
open scoped Nat Topology

namespace Erdos50

/--
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is the asymptotic distribution function of the values
of $\varphi(n)/n$ if for all $c \in [0, 1]$, the natural density of $\{n : \varphi(n) < cn\}$
exists and equals $f(c)$.
-/
def IsDistributionOfPhiRatio (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ c ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, {n : ℕ | (φ n : ℝ) < c * n}.HasDensity (f c)

/--
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is purely singular (or singular continuous) on a set
$s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ if it is continuous on $s$ and its derivative within $s$ equals zero
almost everywhere on $s$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.
-/
def IsPurelySingularOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContinuousOn f s ∧ ∀ᵐ x ∂(volume.restrict s), derivWithin f s x = 0

/--
Schoenberg [Sch38] proved that the asymptotic distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$ exists.
That is, for any $c \in [0, 1]$, the proportion of integers $n \le N$ satisfying $\varphi(n)/n < c$
approaches a limit as $N \to \infty$. This limit function is the cumulative distribution function
of the values of $\varphi(n)/n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50_schoenberg : ∃ f : ℝ → ℝ, IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős [Er95] proved that the distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$ is purely singular on
$[0, 1]$: it is continuous there, but its derivative is zero almost everywhere on $[0, 1]$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50_singular (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f) :
    IsPurelySingularOn f (Icc 0 1) := by
  sorry

/--
Let $f$ be the asymptotic distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$, so that for each $c \in [0,1]$,
$f(c)$ is the natural density of $\{n : \varphi(n) < cn\}$. Is it true that there is no $x$ such
that the derivative $f'(x)$ exists and is positive?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f),
    ¬∃ x ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, ∃ y > 0, HasDerivWithinAt f y (Icc 0 1) x := by
  sorry

end Erdos50

reformulations.difference: Through IsPurelySingularOn, the theorem uses almost-everywhere equality derivWithin f (Icc 0 1) x = 0 without explicitly asserting almost-everywhere differentiability. For arbitrary continuous functions, Mathlib's zero default would make this weaker.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every use of this helper in the file assumes IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f. Inclusion of the cutoff sets and monotonicity of density imply MonotoneOn f (Icc 0 1), hence differentiability almost everywhere. Derivatives within this nondegenerate interval are unique, and agree with ordinary derivatives in its interior; the endpoints are null. Under the actual hypothesis, I proved IsPurelySingularOn f (Icc 0 1) ↔ ContinuousOn f (Icc 0 1) ∧ (∀ᵐ x ∂volume.restrict (Icc 0 1), HasDerivAt f 0 x). Thus the default-value convention does not weaken the source's singularity claim.

reformulations.difference: Lean quantifies over all real-valued extensions of the distribution on [0,1] and uses derivatives within the closed interval, rather than referring informally to the derivative of the unique distribution function.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Uniqueness of density forces all candidate functions to agree on [0,1], so their within-derivatives agree. I proved this independence, the equivalence between quantifying over all candidates and choosing any one candidate, and agreement with ordinary derivatives in (0,1). The endpoints introduce no positive finite derivative: the bounded mean of (n/φ(n))² gives f(t)=O(t²), hence right derivative zero at 0; a rough-number density estimate gives 1−f(1−t) ≫ 1/log(1/t), hence infinite left slope at 1. Outside [0,1] the canonical distribution is constant. These endpoint estimates were checked mathematically, not formalized, so the complete equivalence is not marked proved in Lean.

review.notes: Checked both definitions and all three theorems. The answer polarity agrees with the source, which explicitly asks whether there is no finite positive derivative. The website still records the main problem as open. Scratch files in /workspace/review/ compile successfully; equivalence proofs have no sorryAx dependency. Tests include small totients, the zero input, density normalization, and proofs that every distribution candidate has f(0)=0 and f(1)=1. Schoenberg's full text was blocked by AMS/JSTOR, but its stated existence result is explicitly confirmed by Erdős (1995), p. 171, and the problem page. No repository files were edited.
